title: Accessibility
description: Why accessibility matters for New York State, the standards NYSDS meets, what its components handle for you, and what's still on you.

presets.title: Who accessibility serves
presets.description: More than one in four adult New Yorkers report a disability, and the share climbs with age.
presets.html:
More than one in four adult New Yorkers report a disability

People can't shop around for another DMV or another benefits office. When a state service fails someone online, they can lose access to a service they need.

28.3% of New York adults, about 4 million people, report a disability

42% of New Yorkers age 65 and older report a disability

58.8% of adults with household income under $15,000 report a disability

It also serves people without a disability

A temporary limit, such as a broken arm or lost glasses A situational limit, such as bright sunlight or a place where you can't play sound Abilities that change as people age

Sources: New York State Department of Health, 2022 survey data. W3C Web Accessibility Initiative.

Accessibility docs
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is showing, press c to hide it. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

Start with people, not law. Ask the room who expects to turn 65 someday.

Say:
- More than one in four adults in New York report a disability. That's about 4 million people.
- It climbs with age: 22.1% of adults 18 to 44, and 42% of adults 65 and older.
- It's highest among the people with the least money: 58.8% of adults with household income under $15,000.
- People can't pick a different state government. If our service fails them online, they can lose access to a service they need.
- It also helps people with no disability at all: a broken arm, lost glasses, glare on a phone, a quiet room where you can't play sound.

Sources:
- New York State Department of Health, BRFSS Brief No. 2024-17, "Disability Status, New York State Adults, 2022." 28.3% of adults (about 4.0 million) report a disability; 22.1% of adults 18 to 44; 42.0% of adults 65 and older; 58.8% with annual household income under $15,000. https://health.ny.gov/statistics/brfss/reports/docs/2024-17_brfss_disability_status.pdf
- CDC, "Disability Impacts All of Us": more than 1 in 4 U.S. adults have some type of disability. https://www.cdc.gov/disability-and-health/articles-documents/disability-impacts-all-of-us-infographic.html
- W3C WAI, "Introduction to Web Accessibility" (updated February 3, 2026): accessibility also benefits older people with changing abilities, people with temporary disabilities such as a broken arm or lost glasses, and people with situational limitations such as bright sunlight or a place where they can't listen to audio. https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/
- WHO, "Disability" fact sheet (March 7, 2023): an estimated 1.3 billion people, 16% of the world's population, experience significant disability. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/disability-and-health
- NYSDS, Accessibility: https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/

presets.title: The web still fails the basics
presets.description: In 2026, 95.9% of the top million home pages failed accessibility checks that a tool can detect.
presets.html:
Most of the web fails checks a machine can catch

95.9% of the top million home pages had detectable WCAG failures in February 2026, up from 94.8% in 2025

Why now: ITS policy requires every state agency website to meet WCAG 2.2 AA by January 1, 2027.

The six most common failures, and where NYSDS helps
FailurePagesWhere NYSDS helps
Low-contrast text83.9%NYSDS text tokens
Missing alt text53.1%Up to you
Missing form labels51%NYSDS form components, with a label
Empty links46.3%Up to you
Empty buttons30.6%NYSDS buttons, with a label
Missing page language13.5%Up to you

Source: WebAIM Million, February 2026.
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is showing, press c to hide it. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

WebAIM runs its WAVE engine on the home pages of the top million websites every year. These are only the failures a tool can detect, so real conformance is worse: WebAIM puts full WCAG A and AA conformance below 4.1%.

Point at the last column. NYSDS helps with three of the six when you use its tokens and components, and the next section demos each one. The other three are up to you, and they come back at the end of the deck.

The NYSDS rows depend on you. Text tokens only help if you pick them by role, and a nys-button with no label is still an empty button.

Why now: ITS policy NYS-P08-005, section 4.3, requires each website a state entity owns or maintains, including ones third parties provide, to conform to WCAG 2.2 AA by January 1, 2027, "in accordance with STL Section 103-d." The statute itself is narrower: it covers new sites and sites with changes to form or function, and an agency that can't comply by that date posts a public progress report. The next section covers the rules.

If someone says government sites must be better: .gov home pages averaged 18.5 detected errors, against 56.1 for all home pages. Better, not zero.

For developers who want to hand-roll ARIA: home pages that used ARIA averaged 59.1 detected errors, against 42 for pages without it.

Sources:
- WebAIM, "The WebAIM Million," results from February 2026: 95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures (94.8% in 2025); full conformance "certainly lower than 4.1%"; low-contrast text 83.9%, missing alternative text 53.1%, missing form input labels 51%, empty links 46.3%, empty buttons 30.6%, missing document language 13.5%; .gov averaged 18.5 errors per page against 56.1 overall; pages with ARIA averaged 59.1 errors against 42 without. https://webaim.org/projects/million/
- ITS policy NYS-P08-005, section 4.3: each state entity website, including those provided by third parties, conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA by January 1, 2027. https://its.ny.gov/document/accessibility-web-based-information-and-applications-compliance-reporting

presets.title: WCAG 2.2 Level AA
presets.description: NYSDS builds every component to WCAG 2.2 Level AA, the level New York State requires.
presets.html:
NYSDS builds to WCAG 2.2, Level AA

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the standard that laws and policies point to. Version 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since October 5, 2023, and its success criteria fall under four principles.

Accessibility docs
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is showing, press c to hide it. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

Say:
- WCAG comes from the W3C. Laws don't invent their own technical rules; they point to WCAG.
- Version 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on October 5, 2023. It's also an ISO standard, ISO/IEC 40500:2025.
- Level AA is the line every rule on the next slide draws. AAA is aspirational, not a blanket requirement.
- WCAG is backward compatible. Meet 2.2 AA and you also meet 2.1 AA and 2.0 AA.

If someone asks what 2.2 added at Levels A and AA: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum), Consistent Help, Redundant Entry, and Accessible Authentication (Minimum). It also removed 4.1.1 Parsing. Target size gets its own demo later in this deck.

NYSDS says every component meets WCAG 2.2 AA, works at 200% zoom with no loss of content, and is tested with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver on desktop and mobile.

Sources:
- W3C, WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, current version dated December 12, 2024): https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- W3C WAI, WCAG 2 Overview: WCAG 2.2 published October 5, 2023; backward compatible; approved as ISO/IEC 40500:2025. https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/
- NYSDS, Accessibility: POUR principles, "WCAG 2.2 AA compliant," 200% zoom, NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/ (The Robust card leaves out the page's "valid markup," because WCAG 2.2 removed 4.1.1 Parsing.)
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Leadership: Level A is the minimum, AA is the target for government, AAA is aspirational. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/leadership/

presets.title: The rules for a state agency
presets.description: State law and ITS policy require WCAG 2.2 AA, and building to it also meets the federal ADA rule.
presets.html:
Three rules, one target: WCAG 2.2 AA

Accessibility rules for New York State agency websites
RuleStandardWhat it requiresKey date
NYS Technology Law § 103-d Current WCAG AA (2.2) New agency websites, and sites with changes to form or function, meet the current WCAG at Level AA, to the extent practicable. An agency that can't comply posts a public progress report and updates it every year. January 1, 2027
ITS policy NYS-P08-005 WCAG 2.2 AA Manual testing before launch, before major changes, and every two years. An "Accessibility" link in the footer of every home page. Updated October 7, 2026
ADA Title II rule, 28 CFR Part 35 WCAG 2.1 AA Web content, including documents, and mobile apps from state and local governments. April 26, 2027

WCAG is backward compatible: content that meets 2.2 AA also meets 2.1 AA and 2.0 AA.

Section 508 binds federal agencies and uses WCAG 2.0 AA. When you buy software, ask for WCAG 2.2 AA.

Accessibility for leadership docs
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is showing, press c to hide it. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

Don't get lost in deadline math. The point is the title: build to WCAG 2.2 AA once and every rule on this slide is covered. The countdown is live, so it stays right whenever you present.

Say:
- State law, § 103-d: new state agency websites, and existing ones with "changes to form or function," must conform to the most current WCAG at Level AA, to the extent practicable. ITS reads that as WCAG 2.2 AA. An agency that can't comply by January 1, 2027 must post a public progress report and update it every year.
- ITS policy NYS-P08-005 sets WCAG 2.2 AA for every state entity, including sites that vendors build or run. It also requires manual testing before production use, before fundamental changes, and every two years after that; a list of each system and its status; and an "Accessibility" footer link on the home page.
- The federal ADA Title II rule requires WCAG 2.1 AA for web content and mobile apps of state and local governments. In April 2026, the DOJ moved the date for large governments from April 24, 2026 to April 26, 2027. New York State counts as a large government.
- Section 508 sits under the table because it doesn't bind the state. It applies to federal agencies, and it matters here through procurement: vendors' conformance reports often cite it, and its standard is WCAG 2.0 AA. NYSDS recommends asking for WCAG 2.2 AA instead. The Access Board issued the revised standards on January 18, 2017.

If someone asks about vendors: Executive Law § 170-f puts the same duty on contractors, subcontractors, and vendors. Websites they provide under a state contract must conform to the most current WCAG.

If your agency gets HHS funding, such as DOH, OMH, or OTDA: the HHS Section 504 rule also requires WCAG 2.1 AA for web content and mobile apps. An interim final rule (FR Doc. 2026-09266) moved the date for recipients with 15 or more employees from May 11, 2026 to May 11, 2027. Check with your counsel about which federal rules apply to your programs.

Check before you present: the National Federation of the Blind sued in May 2026 to restore the original ADA dates. As of November 2026, the April 26, 2027 date stands. Check ada.gov for changes.

Discrepancy to know about: a footnote in the ITS policy gives the new DOJ date as April 24, 2027. The Federal Register and ada.gov say April 26, 2027.

Sources:
- NYS Technology Law § 103-d: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/STT/103-D
- Chapter 734 of the Laws of 2023 (A266A), signed December 22, 2023: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2023/A266
- Chapter 42 of the Laws of 2024 (A8546/S8032), a chapter amendment signed February 7, 2024, that sets the January 1, 2027 date and Level AA: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2023/S8032 and https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2023/A8546
- NYS Executive Law § 170-f (state contractors and vendors): https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/EXC/170-F
- Federal Register, HHS Office for Civil Rights, "Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services..." (FR Doc. 2026-09266, published May 11, 2026, effective May 7, 2026): 45 CFR 84.84, WCAG 2.1 Level AA; May 11, 2026 to May 11, 2027 for recipients with 15 or more employees; May 10, 2027 to May 10, 2028 for fewer than 15. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-11/html/2026-09266.htm
- ITS policy NYS-P08-005, "Accessibility of Information Communication Technology," updated October 7, 2026: https://its.ny.gov/document/accessibility-web-based-information-and-applications-compliance-reporting
- Federal Register, "Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities," April 20, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-07663): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/20/2026-07663/extension-of-compliance-dates-for-nondiscrimination-on-the-basis-of-disability-accessibility-of-web
- ADA.gov, Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps: WCAG 2.1 AA; April 26, 2027 for 50,000 or more people; April 26, 2028 for smaller governments and special districts. https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/
- ADA.gov, Small Entity Compliance Guide: a part of a larger government uses the population of the government it belongs to. https://www.ada.gov/resources/small-entity-compliance-guide/
- U.S. Access Board, ICT final rule (January 18, 2017): applies to federal agencies and incorporates WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA. https://www.access-board.gov/ict/
- Route Fifty, "Disability advocates sue over website accessibility delays" (May 2026): https://www.route-fifty.com/customer-experience/2026/05/disability-advocates-sue-over-website-accessibility-delays/413781/
- W3C WAI, WCAG 2 Overview (backward compatibility): https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Leadership (RFP language): https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/leadership/

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: Keyboard and visible focus
presets.description: Tab through both panels: the div never gets focus, and only nys-button shows where focus is.
presets.html:
Every control works from the keyboard

Click the space above this heading, then press Tab. The first stop is a skip link that jumps past navigation to the main content.

Before: hand-rolled

Submit application

Nothing activated yet.

After: nys-button

Nothing activated yet.

Docs: Button · Skip navigation
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is hidden, press c to show it. The demos from here through slide 11 use the code.

Do:
1. Click the white space above the heading, then press Tab. "Skip to main content" appears at the top left. (If you click lower on the slide, Tab starts from where you clicked and passes the skip link.) Press Enter to jump to the main content.
2. Press Tab. Focus skips "Submit application" on the left, because it's a div. It lands on "Save draft," but you can't see it, because its focus ring was removed.
3. Press Enter. The log says "Save draft activated with the keyboard," so focus was there all along. A sighted keyboard user had no way to know.
4. Press Tab into the right panel. Each nys-button shows a clear focus ring. Press Enter or Space, and the log says "activated with the keyboard."
5. Click the left "Submit application" with the mouse to show it only works for mouse users.

Optional: in the CSS, delete the .no-ring:focus rule and the ring comes back. Removing focus styles is a choice someone made.

Say: keyboard access isn't only for blind users. People with tremors, people who use switch devices or voice control, and power users all rely on it.

WCAG: 2.1.1 Keyboard (A), 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA), 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (A) for the skip link.

Sources:
- NYSDS, Accessibility: "All components are fully operable without a mouse," and "Every interactive element has a visible focus indicator." https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/
- NYSDS MCP, nys-button: nys-click fires for mouse and keyboard activation. NYSDS MCP page-structure guide: nys-skipnav is the first focusable element and targets #main-content.
- NYSDS, Skip navigation: https://designsystem.ny.gov/components/skipnav/
- W3C, WCAG 2.2: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: Labels and accessible names
presets.description: A word near a field isn't a label, and an icon isn't a name; NYSDS components fix both.
presets.html:
Every control gets a name

Screen readers announce a control's name, and voice control users say it out loud to click. Both sides look labeled. Only one side is.

Before: hand-rolled

Search the site
Search field name
None
Button name
None

After: nys-textinput and nys-button

Search field name
"Search the site"
Button name
"Search"

Docs: Text input · Button
presets.notes:
Do:
1. Point out that both sides look the same: a word above a field, and a magnifying glass button.
2. Read the gray boxes. The left field and button have no accessible name. A screen reader says something like "search text field" and "button," and stops.
3. Optional: turn on VoiceOver (Command+F5 on a Mac) or NVDA and Tab through both sides.
4. Optional: with Voice Control, say "Click Search." It works on the right and fails on the left, because the left button has no name to match.

Say:
- On the left, the words "Search the site" sit near the field, but no code connects them. The icon-only button has no text at all.
- On the right, the label property becomes the field's name. The circle button shows only an icon, and its label property still gives it the name "Search."
- These are two of the top six failures on the WebAIM slide: missing form labels and empty buttons.

Placeholder text doesn't count as a label. NYSDS says not to use it as a replacement.

WCAG: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A), 2.5.3 Label in Name (A), 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (A), 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A).

Sources:
- NYSDS MCP, nys-textinput: label is "Visible label text. Required for accessibility." Placeholder: "Don't use as label replacement." The endButton slot holds a single nys-button.
- NYSDS MCP form-validation guide: form components associate the visible label with the control through aria-labelledby, with no manual wiring.
- NYSDS MCP, nys-button: in circle mode, label "is visually hidden but still exposed to assistive tech as the accessible name."
- NYSDS MCP, nys-icon: an icon with no ariaLabel is hidden from screen readers (aria-hidden="true"), which is why the left button ends up with no name.
- NYSDS, Accessibility: voice control support for Voice Access on Windows and Voice Control on macOS. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/
- WebAIM Million 2026: missing form input labels on 51% of home pages, empty buttons on 30.6%. https://webaim.org/projects/million/

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: Error messages tied to their fields
presets.description: Submit both empty forms: one only turns red, and nys-textinput says what's wrong at the field.
presets.html:
Errors say what's wrong, in words, at the field

Select Continue on each side without typing anything.

Before: hand-rolled

After you submit
The border turns red. No words say what's wrong, and nothing tells a screen reader the field has a problem.

After: nys-textinput

After you submit
Focus moves to the field. The message appears in words, and the field is marked invalid and linked to it.

Docs: Text input · Forms
presets.notes:
Do:
1. Select Continue on the left. The border turns red. Ask the room what's wrong with the field. Nobody can say, and a person who can't see red gets nothing.
2. Select Continue on the right. Focus moves to the field, and "Enter your full name." appears in words under it, with an icon.
3. Type a name on the right and select Continue again. The error clears as you type, and the gray box says the form would submit.
4. Optional: with a screen reader on, focus the right field after the error. It reads the name and says the field is invalid. Whether it also reads the message depends on the screen reader, so try yours before the talk.

Use the Continue button, not Enter. Pressing Enter inside nys-textinput doesn't submit the form; NYSDS leaves that to the app on purpose (ITS-HCD/nysds#1387).

Say: the right side has no validation code. The required attribute and the errorMessage property do the work, and the component wires aria-invalid and the error message to the field.

For longer forms, add an error summary at the top that links to each field. The "Form validation" slide in the Component library deck shows that pattern.

WCAG: 1.4.1 Use of Color (A), 3.3.1 Error Identification (A), 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (A), 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA).

Sources:
- NYSDS, Form Patterns: on submit, "all fields are validated. The first invalid field receives focus," and errorMessage overrides the browser's message. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/forms/
- NYSDS MCP form-validation guide: components set aria-invalid on the control and associate the error message through aria-errormessage, with no manual wiring.
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Developers: "Never rely on color alone to indicate errors." https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/developers/
- ITS-HCD/nysds#1387, "Textinput Enter to Submit Question" (closed): Enter-to-submit is left to the app. https://github.com/ITS-HCD/nysds/issues/1387

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: Contrast from tokens
presets.description: Choose a text token to see its contrast ratio against the page, checked live against WCAG.
presets.html:
Pick tokens by role, and the contrast comes with them

WCAG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text. Each text token's description says what it's safe for.

Application received

We'll email you when a caseworker reviews it.

Tokens docs
presets.notes:
Do:
1. Start on --nys-color-text: 17.22 to 1, passes everything.
2. Choose --nys-color-text-weak: 8.52 to 1, still passes.
3. Choose --nys-color-text-weaker: 4.20 to 1. It fails for body text and passes for large text. Its description already says to avoid it for important content.
4. Choose --nys-color-text-weakest: 1.83 to 1. It fails everything, and its description says it's decorative only.
5. Choose --nys-color-link: 7.04 to 1.

The ratio is measured live from whatever the tokens resolve to, so it follows the theme and the version you load. The numbers in steps 1 through 5 are for the default theme in NYSDS 1.23.1 on a white surface.

Say: you don't need a contrast checker for every pair of colors. Pick the token by what the text is for, and the system has already done the math. The danger is hard-coded colors, which is how 83.9% of home pages end up with low-contrast text.

WCAG: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA): 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text (at least 24 px, or about 18.7 px bold). The large sample uses nys-font-h3, which is 28 px.

Sources:
- NYSDS MCP token descriptions: --nys-color-text "MUST meet WCAG 4.5:1 contrast"; --nys-color-text-weaker "AVOID for important content"; --nys-color-text-weakest "Decorative text only. AVOID for readable content - insufficient contrast."
- NYSDS, Design tokens: https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/tokens/
- W3C, WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum): https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#contrast-minimum
- WebAIM Million 2026: low-contrast text on 83.9% of home pages. https://webaim.org/projects/million/

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: Target size
presets.description: WCAG 2.2 asks for 24-pixel pointer targets; turn on the zones to see where packed icons fail.
presets.html:
Targets big enough to hit

New in WCAG 2.2: a pointer target needs at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough space around it. That helps people with hand tremors, people using a touchscreen, and anyone using one hand.

Before: 16-pixel icons, packed tight

After: nys-button

nys-button comes in three heights, 40, 48, and 56 pixels, and every one clears the minimum.

Button docs
presets.notes:
Do:
1. Try to click the middle icon on the left, quickly, the way a person with a tremor or a phone in one hand would.
2. Turn on "Show 24-pixel target zones." On the left, the dashed circles overlap each other, so the row fails. The right side gets no circles: every button is bigger than 24 by 24 pixels, so it passes outright and the spacing check never applies.

Say:
- Target Size (Minimum) is new in WCAG 2.2, at Level AA. A target can be smaller than 24 by 24 pixels only if it has enough space around it. WCAG checks that by centering a 24-pixel circle on each target.
- A row of tiny icon buttons is one of the most common places this fails: table actions, file lists, and close buttons.
- nys-button's smallest size is 40 pixels tall. You get the spacing without thinking about it.

WCAG: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA).

Sources:
- W3C, WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum): "at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels," with the spacing exception. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#target-size-minimum
- W3C, Understanding 2.5.8: addresses hand tremors and spasticity, and helps touchscreen users, people using one hand, and people with large fingers. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html
- NYSDS MCP, nys-button: size sm is 40px, md is 48px (default), lg is 56px.

presets.group: 3. What the design system does for you
presets.title: What a screen reader gets
presets.description: Both open with a mouse, but only nys-accordion gives a screen reader a name, a role, and a state.
presets.html:
Name, role, and state, built in

A screen reader can only say what the code tells it. NYSDS publishes its accessibility test results: the accordion passes all 10 of its tests, and the modal passes all 28.

Before: hand-rolled

Does NYSDS make my site accessible?
No. It gives you accessible parts. Headings, link text, alt text, and testing are still yours.
Which screen readers does the NYSDS team test with?
NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver, on desktop and mobile.
What a screen reader gets
Plain text. No role, no open or closed state, and Tab skips it.

After: nys-accordion

No. It gives you accessible parts. Headings, link text, alt text, and testing are still yours.

NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver, on desktop and mobile.
What a screen reader gets
A heading, then a button with its name and its state: collapsed or expanded.

Docs: Accordion · Modal
presets.notes:
Do:
1. Click a question on each side. Both open and close with a mouse.
2. Click the white space above the heading, then press Tab. Focus skips the left side completely and lands on the first question on the right.
3. Press Enter or Space to open and close it.
4. Best, if you can: turn on VoiceOver (Command+F5) or NVDA first. On the right you hear the question, "button," and "collapsed" or "expanded." On the left you hear the text and nothing else.

Say:
- Every interactive control has to expose a name, a role, and a state. A div has none of them unless someone adds ARIA and keyboard handling by hand, and gets it right.
- The NYSDS accordion wraps each question in a real heading too, so screen reader users can jump between questions by heading.
- NYSDS publishes test checklists for some components. Anyone on your team can run the same tests, and they work for checking third-party components too.

WCAG: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A), 2.1.1 Keyboard (A), 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A).

Sources:
- NYSDS, Accordion: test status 10 of 10 passing; the checklist expects you to hear the name, the role of button, and the state, expanded or collapsed. https://designsystem.ny.gov/components/accordion/ and https://designsystem.ny.gov/components/accordion/accessibility-tests/
- NYSDS, Modal: test status 28 of 28 passing. https://designsystem.ny.gov/components/modal/
- NYSDS MCP, nys-accordionitem: the toggle button is wrapped in a real heading element, per the WAI-ARIA Accordion pattern, and opens with click, Enter, or Space.
- NYSDS, Accessibility: tested with NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver across desktop and mobile. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/

presets.title: Headings and link text
presets.description: Screen reader users skim by headings and links, so each panel lists what they'd find.
presets.html:
Headings and links are yours to get right

presets.notes:
Do: 1. Read the Before lists. "Renew your permit" looks like a heading but isn't one, so it's missing. "Fees" jumps from the panel's level 2 to level 5. The links list says "Click here" and "Read more," which mean nothing out of context. 2. Read the After lists: two headings in order, and two links that make sense alone. 3. Live fix: in the Before HTML, replace

Most people renew online. Click here.

with

Most people renew their permit online.

The links list updates when the preview reloads. 4. Optional: change the Before

to an

and watch it join the headings list. Say: - A component can't know what your page is about. Heading levels and link text are content decisions, so they stay with you. - Style and structure are separate in NYSDS. Use the right heading level for the outline, then a nys-font-h* class for the look you want. Both sides of this slide look the same; only the structure differs. - Empty links were on 46.3% of the top million home pages. Vague links like "Click here" don't show up in that count, and they fail people too. WCAG: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A), 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (A), 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (AA). Sources: - NYSDS, Accessibility for Developers: one h1 per page and no skipped levels; "Apply for benefits" instead of "Click here"; links should make sense out of context. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/developers/ - NYSDS, Accessibility for Content Creators: "Use real headings, not bold text," and screen reader users often navigate by links alone. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/content/ - NYSDS MCP typography utilities: nys-font-h1 through nys-font-h6 set the type style without changing the element. - WebAIM Million 2026: empty links on 46.3% of home pages. https://webaim.org/projects/million/

presets.title: Alt text, page titles, and plain language
presets.description: No component can decide what an image means, what a page is called, or how plainly to say it.
presets.html:
Content decisions only you can make

Weak and strong examples
WhatWeakStrong
Alt text alt="chart.png" alt="Chart showing a 15% increase in online benefit applications from 2023 to 2024"
Decorative image alt="blue wave" alt="", so screen readers skip it
Page title <title>Home</title> <title>Renew a permit | Agency name</title>
Page language <html> <html lang="en">
Plain language Applications must be submitted by March 15. Submit your application by March 15.
Word choice Commence, utilize, facilitate Start, use, help

Accessibility for content creators docs
presets.notes:
Press c to hide the code drawer again. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

Say:
- Alt text describes what an image communicates, not what it looks like. A decorative image gets an empty alt so screen readers skip it.
- Every page needs a unique title that says what the page is and who runs it. It's the first thing a screen reader reads, and it's the label on the browser tab.
- lang="en" on the html element tells a screen reader which voice and pronunciation to use. It was missing on 13.5% of the top million home pages.
- NYSDS treats plain language as an accessibility requirement, not a style preference. Clear writing helps people with cognitive and learning disabilities, and it helps everyone else too.

Documents count too. The ADA rule covers PDFs and other documents, and an inaccessible PDF on an accessible site is still a barrier.

WCAG: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (A), 2.4.2 Page Titled (A), 3.1.1 Language of Page (A). Plain language maps to 3.1.5 Reading Level (AAA), and NYSDS asks for it anyway.

Sources:
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Content Creators: plain language is "an accessibility requirement, not a style preference"; "Start" instead of "commence," "Use" instead of "utilize," "Help" instead of "facilitate"; the active-voice March 15 example; the 15% chart alt text example; decorative images need empty alt text. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/content/
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Developers: alt="" on decorative images; set lang on the html element; every page needs a unique, descriptive title. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/developers/
- NYSDS MCP page-structure guide: include a descriptive title with page name and agency, for example "Page Title | Agency Name."
- WebAIM Million 2026: missing alt text on 53.1% of home pages; missing document language on 13.5%. https://webaim.org/projects/million/

presets.title: Test it three ways
presets.description: A keyboard pass, a screen reader pass, and automated checks each find what the others miss.
presets.html:
Test with your hands, your ears, and a tool

29% of 143 planted barriers got past all 10 automated tools combined (UK government test, 2017)

ITS policy NYS-P08-005 requires manual testing before launch, before major changes, and every two years.

Accessibility for developers docs
presets.notes:
If the code drawer is showing, press c to hide it. Nothing on this slide needs the code.

Say:
- Tools are a spell checker, not an editor. In the UK Government Digital Service test, 29% of the barriers got past all 10 tools combined. The best single tool flagged 41%, and only when you count its prompts to check something by hand.
- A keyboard pass needs no software, so anyone on the team can do it on every pull request.
- NYSDS asks you to test with at least NVDA on Windows and VoiceOver on a Mac.
- ITS policy makes manual testing a requirement, not a nice-to-have: before production, before major changes, and every two years, with a written report you keep until the next round.

Also worth a pass: zoom the browser to 200% and narrow the window to 320 pixels wide. Content should reflow without sideways scrolling.

Next steps for the room:
- NYSDS publishes accessibility test checklists for several components, starting with the accordion, at designsystem.ny.gov.
- Join the ITS accessibility community: https://on.ny.gov/a11yteam
- Questions about the policy: accessibilityteam@its.ny.gov

Sources:
- UK Government Digital Service, "What we found when we tested tools on the world's least-accessible webpage" (February 24, 2017): 143 barriers; best tool 41% counting manual-inspection prompts; 29% missed by every tool. https://accessibility.blog.gov.uk/2017/02/24/what-we-found-when-we-tested-tools-on-the-worlds-least-accessible-webpage/
- NYSDS, Accessibility for Developers: Accessibility Insights and NVDA as the primary tools; axe, Lighthouse, WAVE; Pa11y in CI; "Test at minimum with NVDA on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS"; VoiceOver with Cmd+F5. https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/developers/
- ITS policy NYS-P08-005, section 4.3: manual testing before production use, prior to any fundamental alterations, and biennially; documented testing reports. https://its.ny.gov/document/accessibility-web-based-information-and-applications-compliance-reporting
- NYSDS, Accessibility: ITS Accessibility Community link (on.ny.gov/a11yteam). https://designsystem.ny.gov/foundations/accessibility/
- ITS policy NYS-P08-005, section 7.0: inquiries go to accessibilityteam@its.ny.gov. https://its.ny.gov/document/accessibility-web-based-information-and-applications-compliance-reporting
